title: A Player That Moves
summary: Delve is turn-based on a grid: each key press moves the player one tile, and the world (monsters, doors) responds. This lesson connects lesson 10.05's input actions to movement, handles walls, doors and stairs, adds key repeat for held keys, and makes moves look smooth by sliding between tiles in the renderer only.
markdown:
## Turns on a grid Many roguelike games, Delve included, are **turn-based**: nothing in the world happens until the player acts, then every monster takes its turn. The game loop still runs at 60 frames per second (input, animation and drawing need it), but the **game rules** advance one turn per player action. ```mermaid flowchart LR W["Wait for an action
(the loop keeps drawing)"] --> P["Player acts:
move, attack, use item"] P --> M["Each monster acts
(lesson 11.04)"] M --> C["Check: dead? stairs?
(lessons 11.05, 11.06)"] C --> W ``` ## Actions and moves Using lesson 10.05's input map, the movement actions become a direction: ```cpp-norun struct Dir { int dx; int dy; }; std::optional movementFrom(const InputMap& in) { if (in.pressed(Action::Up)) return Dir{ 0, -1 }; if (in.pressed(Action::Down)) return Dir{ 0, 1 }; if (in.pressed(Action::Left)) return Dir{ -1, 0 }; if (in.pressed(Action::Right)) return Dir{ 1, 0 }; return std::nullopt; } ``` Bindings put both the arrow keys and WASD on these actions, and a gamepad's d-pad later just adds more bindings. ## Moving into a tile What happens depends on what is in the target tile. Keeping the decision in one function makes the rules easy to read and test: | Target | Result | Takes a turn? | |---|---|---| | Floor | Move there | Yes | | Stairs | Move there; the level is complete (lesson 11.06) | Yes | | Closed door | The door opens and becomes floor; the player stays | Yes | | Wall, or outside the map | Nothing: a bump | No | | A monster | Attack it instead of moving (lesson 11.05) | Yes | A bump not costing a turn matters for feel: walking into a wall by mistake should not let monsters catch up. The practice task implements this table as `tryMove`. ## Holding a key Pressing an arrow for every step is tiring in long corridors. Holding the key should repeat the move, after a short delay, at a steady rate: ```cpp-norun // A held movement key repeats: the first move on press, then after 0.25 s, then every 0.08 s. if (auto dir{ movementFrom(input) }) { tryMove(*dir); m_repeatTimer = 0.25; m_heldDir = *dir; } else if (heldDirection(input) == m_heldDir) { m_repeatTimer -= dt; if (m_repeatTimer <= 0) { tryMove(m_heldDir); m_repeatTimer += 0.08; } } ``` The update runs at a fixed step, so the repeat rate is the same on every machine (lesson 10.02). ## Smooth movement, without changing the rules The player's **logical** position is a whole tile: the rules (collision, monster AI, saving) only ever see whole tiles. To avoid the character teleporting a tile at a time on screen, the renderer draws it sliding from the previous tile to the current one over a short time: ```cpp-norun // In the player's state: int x, y; int fromX, fromY; float slide; (slide goes 0 → 1 after each move) const float t{ std::min(player.slide, 1.0f) }; const float drawX{ (player.fromX + (player.x - player.fromX) * t) * kTile }; const float drawY{ (player.fromY + (player.y - player.fromY) * t) * kTile }; ``` This is lesson 10.02's interpolation applied to a turn-based game: the simulation is exact and simple, and only the picture is smooth. The camera follows the drawn position, not the logical one, so it glides too. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Letting a bump cost a turn > Players feel cheated when walking into a wall lets monsters move. Only real actions take turns. > [!warning] Mixing drawn and logical positions > Collision and AI must use the whole-tile position; only rendering uses the sliding one. > [!warning] Moving on `held` without a repeat timer > The player rushes across the map at 60 tiles per second. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does "turn-based on a real-time loop" mean for Delve? - The game pauses its loop until a key is pressed - Monsters act every frame and the player acts once per second + The loop runs every frame, but rules advance only when the player acts - Two loops run on separate threads, one for turns and one for drawing > The window stays responsive and animated even while the world waits for the player. ? Which moves cost a turn? - Every key press, including bumping into a wall - Only attacking + Moving, opening a door and attacking; not bumping a wall - Only moving onto a new tile > A wasted bump that let monsters act would feel unfair. ? How does the renderer make tile-by-tile movement look smooth? - It moves the player one pixel per turn - It changes the player's tile position gradually over several turns - It runs the game rules at 60 turns per second + It slides the player's picture from the old tile to the new > The sliding position is only used for drawing; the rules still see the player on whole tiles. ? The player walks into a wall. What should happen? + Nothing, and no turn passes - The player moves into the wall - A turn passes but the player stays still > Bumps should be free, so mistakes do not let monsters act. ? What does walking into a closed door do in Delve? - Moves the player through it + Opens it, using the turn - Nothing at all happens > Opening and passing are separate actions. ? Why is the sliding position used only for drawing? - Because floats cannot be compared - To save memory + The rules stay exact on whole tiles > It is interpolation for presentation only. ```
ideas:
- Add diagonal movement on the Q, E, Z and C keys. Should moving diagonally between two walls be allowed?
- Make the slide take 0.1 s and then 0.3 s, and decide which feels better.
- Add a "wait" action (the full stop key) that passes a turn without moving.

cards.q: What does "turn-based on a real-time loop" mean for Delve?
cards.a:
The loop runs every frame, but rules advance only when the player acts

The window stays responsive and animated even while the world waits for the player.

Moving, opening a door and attacking; not bumping a wall

A wasted bump that let monsters act would feel unfair.

cards.q: How does the renderer make tile-by-tile movement look smooth?
cards.a:
It slides the player's picture from the old tile to the new

The sliding position is only used for drawing; the rules still see the player on whole tiles.

cards.q: The player walks into a wall. What should happen?
cards.a:
Nothing, and no turn passes

Bumps should be free, so mistakes do not let monsters act.

cards.q: What does walking into a closed door do in Delve?
cards.a:
Opens it, using the turn

Opening and passing are separate actions.

cards.q: Why is the sliding position used only for drawing?
cards.a:
The rules stay exact on whole tiles

It is interpolation for presentation only.
